Cutty Sark: the fastest sailing ship of all time
The nineteenth century was a period of great technological development in Britain, and for
shipping the major changes were from wind to steam power, and from wood to iron and steel.
The fastest commercial sailing vessels of all time were clippers, three-masted ships built to
transport goods around the world, although some also took passengers. From the 1840s until
1869, when the Suez Canal opened and steam propulsion was replacing sail, clippers dominated
world trade. Although many were built, only one has survived more or less intact: Cutty Sark,
now on display in Greenwich, southeast London.
Cutty Sark’s unusual name comes from the poem Tam O’Shanter by the Scottish poet Robert
Burns. Tam, a farmer, is chased by a witch called Nannie, who is wearing a ‘cutty sark’ – an
old Scottish name for a short nightdress. The witch is depicted in Cutty Sark’s figurehead – the
carving of a woman typically at the front of old sailing ships. In legend, and in Burns’s poem,
witches cannot cross water, so this was a rather strange choice of name for a ship.
Cutty Sark was built in Dumbarton, Scotland, in 1869, for a shipping company owned by John
Willis. To carry out construction, Willis chose a new shipbuilding firm, Scott & Linton, and
ensured that the contract with them put him in a very strong position. In the end, the firm was
forced out of business, and the ship was finished by a competitor.
Willis’s company was active in the tea trade between China and Britain, where speed could
bring shipowners both profits and prestige, so Cutty Sark was designed to make the journey
more quickly than any other ship. On her maiden voyage, in 1870, she set sail from London,
carrying large amounts of goods to China. She returned laden with tea, making the journey back
to London in four months. However, Cutty Sark never lived up to the high expectations of her
owner, as a result of bad winds and various misfortunes. On one occasion, in 1872, the ship and
a rival clipper, Thermopylae, left port in China on the same day. Crossing the Indian Ocean,
Cutty Sark gained a lead of over 400 miles, but then her rudder was severely damaged in stormy
seas, making her impossible to steer. The ship’s crew had the daunting task of repairing the
rudder at sea, and only succeeded at the second attempt. Cutty Sark reached London a week after
Thermopylae.

Steam ships posed a growing threat to clippers, as their speed and cargo capacity increased. In
addition, the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, the same year that Cutty Sark was launched,
had a serious impact. While steam ships could make use of the quick, direct route between the
Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the canal was of no use to sailing ships, which needed the much
stronger winds of the oceans, and so had to sail a far greater distance. Steam ships reduced the
journey time between Britain and China by approximately two months.
By 1878, tea traders weren’t interested in Cutty Sark, and instead, she took on the much less
prestigious work of carrying any cargo between any two ports in the world. In 1880, violence
aboard the ship led ultimately to the replacement of the captain with an incompetent drunkard
who stole the crew’s wages. He was suspended from service, and a new captain appointed. This
marked a turnaround and the beginning of the most successful period in Cutty Sark’s working
life, transporting wool from Australia to Britain. One such journey took just under 12 weeks,
beating every other ship sailing that year by around a month.
The ship’s next captain, Richard Woodget, was an excellent navigator, who got the best out of
both his ship and his crew. As a sailing ship, Cutty Sark depended on the strong trade winds of the
southern hemisphere, and Woodget took her further south than any previous captain, bringing her
dangerously close to icebergs off the southern tip of South America. His gamble paid off, though,
and the ship was the fastest vessel in the wool trade for ten years.
As competition from steam ships increased in the 1890s, and Cutty Sark approached the end of
her life expectancy, she became less profitable. She was sold to a Portuguese firm, which renamed
her Ferreira. For the next 25 years, she again carried miscellaneous cargoes around the world.
Badly damaged in a gale in 1922, she was put into Falmouth harbour in southwest England, for
repairs. Wilfred Dowman, a retired sea captain who owned a training vessel, recognised her and
tried to buy her, but without success. She returned to Portugal and was sold to another Portuguese
company. Dowman was determined, however, and offered a high price: this was accepted, and
the ship returned to Falmouth the following year and had her original name restored.
Dowman used Cutty Sark as a training ship, and she continued in this role after his death. When
she was no longer required, in 1954, she was transferred to dry dock at Greenwich to go on
public display. The ship suffered from fire in 2007, and again, less seriously, in 2014, but now
Cutty Sark attracts a quarter of a million visitors a year.

SAVING THE SOIL
More than a third of the Earth’s top layer is at risk. Is there hope for our planet’s
most precious resource?
A
More than a third of the world’s soil is endangered, according to a recent UN report.
If we don’t slow the decline, all farmable soil could be gone in 60 years. Since soil
grows 95% of our food, and sustains human life in other more surprising ways, that
is a huge problem.
B
Peter Groffman, from the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York, points
out that soil scientists have been warning about the degradation of the world’s soil
for decades. At the same time, our understanding of its importance to humans has
grown. A single gram of healthy soil might contain 100 million bacteria, as well as
other microorganisms such as viruses and fungi, living amid decomposing plants
and various minerals.
That means soils do not just grow our food, but are the source of nearly all our
existing antibiotics, and could be our best hope in the fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Soil is also an ally against climate change: as microorganisms
within soil digest dead animals and plants, they lock in their carbon content, holding
three times the amount of carbon as does the entire atmosphere. Soils also store
water, preventing flood damage: in the UK, damage to buildings, roads and bridges
from floods caused by soil degradation costs £233 million every year.
C
If the soil loses its ability to perform these functions, the human race could be in
big trouble. The danger is not that the soil will disappear completely, but that the
microorganisms that give it its special properties will be lost. And once this has
happened, it may take the soil thousands of years to recover.
Agriculture is by far the biggest problem. In the wild, when plants grow they remove
nutrients from the soil, but then when the plants die and decay these nutrients are
returned directly to the soil. Humans tend not to return unused parts of harvested
crops directly to the soil to enrich it, meaning that the soil gradually becomes
less fertile. In the past we developed strategies to get around the problem, such
as regularly varying the types of crops grown, or leaving fields uncultivated for a
season.
D
But these practices became inconvenient as populations grew and agriculture had
to be run on more commercial lines. A solution came in the early 20th century with
the Haber-Bosch process for manufacturing ammonium nitrate. Farmers have been
putting this synthetic fertiliser on their fields ever since.
85

But over the past few decades, it has become clear this wasn’t such a bright idea.
Chemical fertilisers can release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere and
excess is often washed away with the rain, releasing nitrogen into rivers. More
recently, we have found that indiscriminate use of fertilisers hurts the soil itself,
turning it acidic and salty, and degrading the soil they are supposed to nourish.
E
One of the people looking for a solution to this problem is Pius Floris, who started
out running a tree-care business in the Netherlands, and now advises some of the
world’s top soil scientists. He came to realise that the best way to ensure his trees
flourished was to take care of the soil, and has developed a cocktail of beneficial
bacteria, fungi and humus* to do this. Researchers at the University of Valladolid in
Spain recently used this cocktail on soils destroyed by years of fertiliser overuse.
When they applied Floris’s mix to the desert-like test plots, a good crop of plants
emerged that were not just healthy at the surface, but had roots strong enough to
pierce dirt as hard as rock. The few plants that grew in the control plots, fed with
traditional fertilisers, were small and weak.
F
However, measures like this are not enough to solve the global soil degradation
problem. To assess our options on a global scale we first need an accurate picture
of what types of soil are out there, and the problems they face. That’s not easy. For
one thing, there is no agreed international system for classifying soil. In an attempt
to unify the different approaches, the UN has created the Global Soil Map project.
Researchers from nine countries are working together to create a map linked to a
database that can be fed measurements from field surveys, drone surveys, satellite
imagery, lab analyses and so on to provide real-time data on the state of the soil.
Within the next four years, they aim to have mapped soils worldwide to a depth of
100 metres, with the results freely accessible to all.
G
But this is only a first step. We need ways of presenting the problem that bring
it home to governments and the wider public, says Pamela Chasek at the
International Institute for Sustainable Development, in Winnipeg, Canada. ‘Most
scientists don’t speak language that policy-makers can understand, and vice versa.’
Chasek and her colleagues have proposed a goal of ‘zero net land degradation’.
Like the idea of carbon neutrality, it is an easily understood target that can help
shape expectations and encourage action.
For soils on the brink, that may be too late. Several researchers are agitating for
the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils. One difficulty
here is defining what these areas should conserve: areas where the greatest soil
diversity is present? Or areas of unspoilt soils that could act as a future benchmark
of quality?
Whatever we do, if we want our soils to survive, we need to take action now.
* Humus: the part of the soil formed from dead plant material

Book Review
The Happiness Industry: How the Government and Big Business
Sold Us Well-Being
By William Davies
‘Happiness is the ultimate goal because it is self-evidently good. If we are asked why
happiness matters we can give no further external reason. It just obviously does matter.’ This
pronouncement by Richard Layard, an economist and advocate of ‘positive psychology’,
summarises the beliefs of many people today. For Layard and others like him, it is obvious that
the purpose of government is to promote a state of collective well-being. The only question is
how to achieve it, and here positive psychology – a supposed science that not only identifies
what makes people happy but also allows their happiness to be measured – can show the way.
Equipped with this science, they say, governments can secure happiness in society in a way they
never could in the past.
It is an astonishingly crude and simple-minded way of thinking, and for that very reason
increasingly popular. Those who think in this way are oblivious to the vast philosophical
literature in which the meaning and value of happiness have been explored and questioned,
and write as if nothing of any importance had been thought on the subject until it came to their
attention. It was the philosopher Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) who was more than anyone else
responsible for the development of this way of thinking. For Bentham it was obvious that the
human good consists of pleasure and the absence of pain. The Greek philosopher Aristotle may
have identified happiness with self-realisation in the 4th century BC, and thinkers throughout the
ages may have struggled to reconcile the pursuit of happiness with other human values, but for
Bentham all this was mere metaphysics or fiction. Without knowing anything much of him or the
school of moral theory he established – since they are by education and intellectual conviction
illiterate in the history of ideas – our advocates of positive psychology follow in his tracks in
rejecting as outmoded and irrelevant pretty much the entirety of ethical reflection on human
happiness to date.
But as William Davies notes in his recent book The Happiness Industry, the view that happiness
is the only self-evident good is actually a way of limiting moral inquiry. One of the virtues of
this rich, lucid and arresting book is that it places the current cult of happiness in a well-defined
historical framework. Rightly, Davies begins his story with Bentham, noting that he was far
more than a philosopher. Davies writes, ‘Bentham’s activities were those which we might now
associate with a public sector management consultant’. In the 1790s, he wrote to the Home Office
suggesting that the departments of government be linked together through a set of ‘conversation
tubes’, and to the Bank of England with a design for a printing device that could produce
89

unforgeable banknotes. He drew up plans for a ‘frigidarium’ to keep provisions such as meat,
fish, fruit and vegetables fresh. His celebrated design for a prison to be known as a ‘Panopticon’,
in which prisoners would be kept in solitary confinement while being visible at all times to the
guards, was very nearly adopted. (Surprisingly, Davies does not discuss the fact that Bentham
meant his Panopticon not just as a model prison but also as an instrument of control that could be
applied to schools and factories.)
Bentham was also a pioneer of the ‘science of happiness’. If happiness is to be regarded as
a science, it has to be measured, and Bentham suggested two ways in which this might be
done. Viewing happiness as a complex of pleasurable sensations, he suggested that it might be
quantified by measuring the human pulse rate. Alternatively, money could be used as the standard
for quantification: if two different goods have the same price, it can be claimed that they produce
the same quantity of pleasure in the consumer. Bentham was more attracted by the latter measure.
By associating money so closely to inner experience, Davies writes, Bentham ‘set the stage for
the entangling of psychological research and capitalism that would shape the business practices
of the twentieth century’.
The Happiness Industry describes how the project of a science of happiness has become
integral to capitalism. We learn much that is interesting about how economic problems are
being redefined and treated as psychological maladies. In addition, Davies shows how the
belief that inner states of pleasure and displeasure can be objectively measured has informed
management studies and advertising. The tendency of thinkers such as J B Watson, the founder
of behaviourism*, was that human beings could be shaped, or manipulated, by policymakers and
managers. Watson had no factual basis for his view of human action. When he became president
of the American Psychological Association in 1915, he ‘had never even studied a single human
being’: his research had been confined to experiments on white rats. Yet Watson’s reductive
model is now widely applied, with ‘behaviour change’ becoming the goal of governments: in
Britain, a ‘Behaviour Insights Team’ has been established by the government to study how people
can be encouraged, at minimum cost to the public purse, to live in what are considered to be
socially desirable ways.
Modern industrial societies appear to need the possibility of ever-increasing happiness to
motivate them in their labours. But whatever its intellectual pedigree, the idea that governments
should be responsible for promoting happiness is always a threat to human freedom.
* ‘behaviourism’: a branch of psychology which is concerned with observable behaviour

His celebrated design for a prison to be known as a ‘Panopticon’, in which prisoners would be kept in solitary confinement while being visible at all times to the guards, was very nearly adopted. (Surprisingly, Davies does not discuss the fact that Bentham meant his Panopticon not just as a model prison but also as an instrument of control that could be applied to schools and factories.)

Bentham was also a pioneer of the ‘science of happiness’. If happiness is to be regarded as a science, it has to be measured, and Bentham suggested two ways in which this might be done. Viewing happiness as a complex of pleasurable sensations, he suggested that it might be quantified by measuring the human pulse rate. Alternatively, money could be used as the standard for quantification: if two different goods have the same price, it can be claimed that they produce the same quantity of pleasure in the consumer. Bentham was more attracted by the latter measure. By associating money so closely to inner experience, Davies writes, Bentham ‘set the stage for the entangling of psychological research and capitalism that would shape the business practices of the twentieth century’.

The Happiness Industry describes how the project of a science of happiness has become integral to capitalism. We learn much that is interesting about how economic problems are being redefined and treated as psychological maladies. In addition, Davies shows how the belief that inner states of pleasure and displeasure can be objectively measured has informed management studies and advertising. The tendency of thinkers such as J B Watson, the founder of behaviourism*, was that human beings could be shaped, or manipulated, by policymakers and managers. Watson had no factual basis for his view of human action. When he became president of the American Psychological Association in 1915, he ‘had never even studied a single human being’: his research had been confined to experiments on white rats. Yet Watson’s reductive model is now widely applied, with ‘behaviour change’ becoming the goal of governments: in Britain, a ‘Behaviour Insights Team’ has been established by the government to study how people can be encouraged, at minimum cost to the public purse, to live in what are considered to be socially desirable ways.

Modern industrial societies appear to need the possibility of ever-increasing happiness to motivate them in their labours. But whatever its intellectual pedigree, the idea that governments should be responsible for promoting happiness is always a threat to human freedom.

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 1
readingSections.titleText: Cutty Sark: the fastest sailing ship of all time
paragraphs: The nineteenth century was a period of great technological development in Britain, and for shipping the major changes were from wind to steam power, and from wood to iron and steel. The fastest commercial sailing vessels of all time were clippers, three-masted ships built to transport goods around the world, although some also took passengers. From the 1840s until 1869, when the Suez Canal opened and steam propulsion was replacing sail, clippers dominated world trade. Although many were built, only one has survived more or less intact: Cutty Sark, now on display in Greenwich, southeast London.

Cutty Sark’s unusual name comes from the poem Tam O’Shanter by the Scottish poet Robert Burns. Tam, a farmer, is chased by a witch called Nannie, who is wearing a ‘cutty sark’ – an old Scottish name for a short nightdress. The witch is depicted in Cutty Sark’s figurehead – the carving of a woman typically at the front of old sailing ships. In legend, and in Burns’s poem, witches cannot cross water, so this was a rather strange choice of name for a ship.

Cutty Sark was built in Dumbarton, Scotland, in 1869, for a shipping company owned by John Willis. To carry out construction, Willis chose a new shipbuilding firm, Scott & Linton, and ensured that the contract with them put him in a very strong position. In the end, the firm was forced out of business, and the ship was finished by a competitor.

Willis’s company was active in the tea trade between China and Britain, where speed could bring shipowners both profits and prestige, so Cutty Sark was designed to make the journey more quickly than any other ship. On her maiden voyage, in 1870, she set sail from London, carrying large amounts of goods to China. She returned laden with tea, making the journey back to London in four months. However, Cutty Sark never lived up to the high expectations of her owner, as a result of bad winds and various misfortunes. On one occasion, in 1872, the ship and a rival clipper, Thermopylae, left port in China on the same day. Crossing the Indian Ocean, Cutty Sark gained a lead of over 400 miles, but then her rudder was severely damaged in stormy seas, making her impossible to steer. The ship’s crew had the daunting task of repairing the rudder at sea, and only succeeded at the second attempt. Cutty Sark reached London a week after Thermopylae.

Steam ships posed a growing threat to clippers, as their speed and cargo capacity increased. In addition, the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, the same year that Cutty Sark was launched, had a serious impact. While steam ships could make use of the quick, direct route between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the canal was of no use to sailing ships, which needed the much stronger winds of the oceans, and so had to sail a far greater distance. Steam ships reduced the journey time between Britain and China by approximately two months.

By 1878, tea traders weren’t interested in Cutty Sark, and instead, she took on the much less prestigious work of carrying any cargo between any two ports in the world. In 1880, violence aboard the ship led ultimately to the replacement of the captain with an incompetent drunkard who stole the crew’s wages. He was suspended from service, and a new captain appointed. This marked a turnaround and the beginning of the most successful period in Cutty Sark’s working life, transporting wool from Australia to Britain. One such journey took just under 12 weeks, beating every other ship sailing that year by around a month.

The ship’s next captain, Richard Woodget, was an excellent navigator, who got the best out of both his ship and his crew. As a sailing ship, Cutty Sark depended on the strong trade winds of the southern hemisphere, and Woodget took her further south than any previous captain, bringing her dangerously close to icebergs off the southern tip of South America. His gamble paid off, though, and the ship was the fastest vessel in the wool trade for ten years.

As competition from steam ships increased in the 1890s, and Cutty Sark approached the end of her life expectancy, she became less profitable. She was sold to a Portuguese firm, which renamed her Ferreira. For the next 25 years, she again carried miscellaneous cargoes around the world. Badly damaged in a gale in 1922, she was put into Falmouth harbour in southwest England, for repairs. Wilfred Dowman, a retired sea captain who owned a training vessel, recognised her and tried to buy her, but without success. She returned to Portugal and was sold to another Portuguese company. Dowman was determined, however, and offered a high price: this was accepted, and the ship returned to Falmouth the following year and had her original name restored.

Dowman used Cutty Sark as a training ship, and she continued in this role after his death. When she was no longer required, in 1954, she was transferred to dry dock at Greenwich to go on public display. The ship suffered from fire in 2007, and again, less seriously, in 2014, but now Cutty Sark attracts a quarter of a million visitors a year.

sentences.text: The nineteenth century was a period of great technological development in Britain, and for shipping the major changes were from wind to steam power, and from wood to iron and steel.
sentences.translation: 十九世纪是英国技术大发展的时期；就航运而言，主要变化是动力从风力转向蒸汽，船体材料从木材转向钢铁。
sentences.structure: 并列主干以 The nineteenth century was... 定位时代，再用 for shipping 限定领域；两组 from...to... 平行呈现动力与材料的技术转型，作为全文历史背景。

sentences.text: The fastest commercial sailing vessels of all time were clippers, three-masted ships built to transport goods around the world, although some also took passengers.
sentences.translation: 有史以来速度最快的商用帆船是快速帆船：这种三桅船为运送世界各地的货物而建，不过有些也载客。
sentences.structure: 主干是 vessels were clippers；同位语 three-masted ships 解释船型，过去分词 built to... 说明目的，although 从句补充例外用途。

sentences.text: From the 1840s until 1869, when the Suez Canal opened and steam propulsion was replacing sail, clippers dominated world trade.
sentences.translation: 从19世纪40年代到1869年苏伊士运河开通、蒸汽推进逐渐取代风帆之时，快速帆船主导着世界贸易。
sentences.structure: 时间介词短语与 when 从句界定时代；主干 clippers dominated world trade 概括其鼎盛，replacing 用进行时突出转型过程。

sentences.text: Although many were built, only one has survived more or less intact: Cutty Sark, now on display in Greenwich, southeast London.
sentences.translation: 尽管建造了许多这样的船，却只有一艘大体完整地保存下来：如今在伦敦东南部格林尼治展出的“卡蒂萨克号”。
sentences.structure: Although 让步从句衬托 only one 的稀有；冒号引出唯一幸存者，now on display 是省略关系结构，交代现状。

sentences.text: Cutty Sark’s unusual name comes from the poem Tam O’Shanter by the Scottish poet Robert Burns.
sentences.translation: “卡蒂萨克号”这个不寻常的名字来自苏格兰诗人罗伯特·彭斯的诗《汤姆·奥桑特》。
sentences.structure: 主干 name comes from the poem；介词短语补出作者身份，作用是解释船名来源。

sentences.text: Tam, a farmer, is chased by a witch called Nannie, who is wearing a ‘cutty sark’ – an old Scottish name for a short nightdress.
sentences.translation: 农夫汤姆被名叫南妮的女巫追赶；她穿着一件“cutty sark”——苏格兰古语中的短睡裙。
sentences.structure: 主干 Tam is chased；同位语 a farmer、called Nannie 与 who 从句层层补充人物，破折号解释苏格兰旧称。

sentences.text: The witch is depicted in Cutty Sark’s figurehead – the carving of a woman typically at the front of old sailing ships.
sentences.translation: 这名女巫被刻画在卡蒂萨克号的船首像上——那通常是旧式帆船前端的女性雕像。
sentences.structure: 被动主干 The witch is depicted；介词短语锁定船首像，破折号后的同位说明其形态和典型位置。

sentences.text: In legend, and in Burns’s poem, witches cannot cross water, so this was a rather strange choice of name for a ship.
sentences.translation: 在传说和彭斯的诗中，女巫不能渡水，所以给船取这个名字颇为奇怪。
sentences.structure: In legend 与 in Burns’s poem 并列限定信息来源；so 引出因果结论，rather 缓和却强化“命名奇怪”的评价。

sentences.text: Cutty Sark was built in Dumbarton, Scotland, in 1869, for a shipping company owned by John Willis.
sentences.translation: 卡蒂萨克号于1869年在苏格兰敦巴顿建造，订造者是约翰·威利斯拥有的一家航运公司。
sentences.structure: 被动主干 Cutty Sark was built；地点、时间、委托对象依次后置，owned by... 说明公司所有权。

sentences.text: To carry out construction, Willis chose a new shipbuilding firm, Scott & Linton, and ensured that the contract with them put him in a very strong position.
sentences.translation: 为实施建造，威利斯选择了新的造船公司 Scott & Linton，并确保与其签订的合同让自己处于非常有利的位置。
sentences.structure: 不定式 To carry out... 前置表目的；两个并列谓语 chose 和 ensured 展示威利斯如何掌控项目，that 从句是 ensured 的宾语。

sentences.text: In the end, the firm was forced out of business, and the ship was finished by a competitor.
sentences.translation: 最终，这家公司被迫停业，船只则由一家竞争对手完工。
sentences.structure: In the end 标示结果；两个被动分句并列，以公司倒闭和对手完工构成因果收束。

sentences.text: Willis’s company was active in the tea trade between China and Britain, where speed could bring shipowners both profits and prestige, so Cutty Sark was designed to make the journey more quickly than any other ship.
sentences.translation: 威利斯的公司活跃于中英茶叶贸易，在这一行业，速度能为船主带来利润和声望，因此卡蒂萨克号被设计成比任何其他船更快完成航程。
sentences.structure: 主干 company was active...，where 从句解释速度的商业价值，so 引出设计目标；比较结构 than any other ship 强调极限追求。

sentences.text: On her maiden voyage, in 1870, she set sail from London, carrying large amounts of goods to China.
sentences.translation: 1870年首航时，它从伦敦扬帆出发，载着大量货物前往中国。
sentences.structure: On her maiden voyage 定位事件；set sail 是主干，carrying 分词结构补充伴随的货物与目的地。

sentences.text: She returned laden with tea, making the journey back to London in four months.
sentences.translation: 它满载茶叶返航，四个月便回到伦敦。
sentences.structure: 主干 She returned；laden with tea 描写满载状态，making 分词结构补充航程用时。

sentences.text: However, Cutty Sark never lived up to the high expectations of her owner, as a result of bad winds and various misfortunes.
sentences.translation: 然而，由于风况不佳和种种不幸，卡蒂萨克号从未达到船主的高期望。
sentences.structure: However 转折；live up to 是主干谓语，as a result of 引出未达预期的原因。

sentences.text: On one occasion, in 1872, the ship and a rival clipper, Thermopylae, left port in China on the same day.
sentences.translation: 有一次是在1872年，它与竞争对手快速帆船“塞莫皮莱号”同日驶离中国港口。
sentences.structure: On one occasion 锁定个案；两个船名组成并列主语，left port 是核心动作，同日出发建立公平竞赛。

sentences.text: Crossing the Indian Ocean, Cutty Sark gained a lead of over 400 miles, but then her rudder was severely damaged in stormy seas, making her impossible to steer.
sentences.translation: 横渡印度洋时，卡蒂萨克号取得了400多英里的领先，但船舵随后在风浪中严重受损，使船无法操纵。
sentences.structure: Crossing... 是时间背景；but 连接领先与受损的逆转，making... 是结果结构，说明损伤使船无法操纵。

sentences.text: The ship’s crew had the daunting task of repairing the rudder at sea, and only succeeded at the second attempt.
sentences.translation: 船员面临在海上修复船舵的艰巨任务，直到第二次尝试才成功。
sentences.structure: 主干 crew had the daunting task；of repairing... 说明任务内容，and 连接结果，only 与 second 突出艰难。

sentences.text: Cutty Sark reached London a week after Thermopylae.
sentences.translation: 卡蒂萨克号比塞莫皮莱号晚一周抵达伦敦。
sentences.structure: 简单主干 Cutty Sark reached London；after Thermopylae 把比赛结局量化为晚一周。

sentences.text: Steam ships posed a growing threat to clippers, as their speed and cargo capacity increased.
sentences.translation: 随着蒸汽船的速度与载货能力提升，它们对快速帆船构成了日益增大的威胁。
sentences.structure: 主干 Steam ships posed...；as 原因从句说明威胁随速度和载货量增长而扩大。

sentences.text: In addition, the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, the same year that Cutty Sark was launched, had a serious impact.
sentences.translation: 此外，1869年苏伊士运河开通——也就是卡蒂萨克号下水的同一年——造成了严重影响。
sentences.structure: In addition 衔接第二重压力；同位插入语把运河开通与下水年份并置，主干 had a serious impact 点明后果。

sentences.text: While steam ships could make use of the quick, direct route between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the canal was of no use to sailing ships, which needed the much stronger winds of the oceans, and so had to sail a far greater distance.
sentences.translation: 蒸汽船可以利用地中海与红海之间快捷而直接的航线；但运河对依赖大洋强风的帆船毫无用处，所以帆船不得不航行远得多的距离。
sentences.structure: While 对比两类船；蒸汽船可走直线，帆船的 which 从句解释其风力需求，and so 推出必须绕远。

sentences.text: Steam ships reduced the journey time between Britain and China by approximately two months.
sentences.translation: 蒸汽船把英国与中国之间的航程缩短了大约两个月。
sentences.structure: 主干 Steam ships reduced...；between... 限定航线，approximately two months 给出幅度，直接支持第6题。

sentences.text: By 1878, tea traders weren’t interested in Cutty Sark, and instead, she took on the much less prestigious work of carrying any cargo between any two ports in the world.
sentences.translation: 到1878年，茶商已对卡蒂萨克号失去兴趣，它转而承担声望低得多的工作，在世界任意两个港口之间运送各种货物。
sentences.structure: By 1878 定位转折时间；and instead 连接“失去茶商订单”与“改运杂货”，less prestigious 作比较评价。

sentences.text: In 1880, violence aboard the ship led ultimately to the replacement of the captain with an incompetent drunkard who stole the crew’s wages.
sentences.translation: 1880年，船上暴力事件最终导致船长被一名无能的酒鬼取代，后者还偷走了船员工资。
sentences.structure: 主干 violence...led...；to the replacement 指结果，with 引出替代者，who 从句追加偷工资的恶行。

sentences.text: He was suspended from service, and a new captain appointed.
sentences.translation: 他被停职，随后任命了一位新船长。
sentences.structure: 两个被动谓语并列但第二个省略 was；句子简洁表现旧船长停职、新船长上任。

sentences.text: This marked a turnaround and the beginning of the most successful period in Cutty Sark’s working life, transporting wool from Australia to Britain.
sentences.translation: 这标志着转机，也开启了卡蒂萨克号营运生涯中最成功的时期：把羊毛从澳大利亚运往英国。
sentences.structure: 主干 This marked...；两个并列宾语是转机与新阶段，transporting... 说明该成功阶段的具体业务。

sentences.text: One such journey took just under 12 weeks, beating every other ship sailing that year by around a month.
sentences.translation: 其中一次航程不足12周，比当年其他所有参航船只快了约一个月。
sentences.structure: 主干 journey took...；beating 分词结构表示结果，与其他船的一个月差距量化优势。

sentences.text: The ship’s next captain, Richard Woodget, was an excellent navigator, who got the best out of both his ship and his crew.
sentences.translation: 下一任船长理查德·伍杰特是一位优秀的领航员，能让船和船员发挥出最佳水平。
sentences.structure: 主干 captain was an excellent navigator；who 从句用 get the best out of 具体说明他的能力。

sentences.text: As a sailing ship, Cutty Sark depended on the strong trade winds of the southern hemisphere, and Woodget took her further south than any previous captain, bringing her dangerously close to icebergs off the southern tip of South America.
sentences.translation: 作为帆船，卡蒂萨克号依赖南半球强劲的信风；伍杰特让它比此前任何船长都驶得更南，危险地接近南美洲南端外海的冰山。
sentences.structure: As 引出船型条件；主干说明依赖信风与船长南下，bringing 分词结构突出随之而来的冰山风险。

sentences.text: His gamble paid off, though, and the ship was the fastest vessel in the wool trade for ten years.
sentences.translation: 不过，他的冒险取得了回报，这艘船连续十年成为羊毛贸易中最快的船。
sentences.structure: 主干 gamble paid off 与 ship was... 并列；though 让步语气承认风险，for ten years 突出优势持续期。

sentences.text: As competition from steam ships increased in the 1890s, and Cutty Sark approached the end of her life expectancy, she became less profitable.
sentences.translation: 随着19世纪90年代蒸汽船竞争加剧，而且卡蒂萨克号接近预期使用寿命终点，它的盈利能力下降。
sentences.structure: As 从句并列交代竞争与船龄两重压力；主干 she became less profitable 给出商业后果。

sentences.text: She was sold to a Portuguese firm, which renamed her Ferreira.
sentences.translation: 它被卖给一家葡萄牙公司，该公司把它改名为“费雷拉号”。
sentences.structure: 被动主干 She was sold；which 非限定从句补充买方改名行为。

sentences.text: For the next 25 years, she again carried miscellaneous cargoes around the world.
sentences.translation: 此后25年，它再次在世界各地运输各种杂货。
sentences.structure: 时间状语 For the next 25 years 框定阶段；主干 carried... 概括全球杂货运输。

sentences.text: Badly damaged in a gale in 1922, she was put into Falmouth harbour in southwest England, for repairs.
sentences.translation: 1922年，它在大风中严重受损，被送进英格兰西南部的法尔茅斯港维修。
sentences.structure: Badly damaged... 是过去分词原因背景；被动主干 she was put into...，for repairs 表目的。

sentences.text: Wilfred Dowman, a retired sea captain who owned a training vessel, recognised her and tried to buy her, but without success.
sentences.translation: 退休船长威尔弗雷德·道曼拥有一艘训练船；他认出了它并试图购买，却没有成功。
sentences.structure: 同位语 a retired sea captain 与 who 从句说明道曼身份；recognised 和 tried 并列，but 转出失败。

sentences.text: She returned to Portugal and was sold to another Portuguese company.
sentences.translation: 它返回葡萄牙，又被卖给另一家葡萄牙公司。
sentences.structure: 两个并列谓语顺序推进船的去向与所有权变化：returned 是不及物动词的一般过去时主动用法，was sold 是被动语态。

sentences.text: Dowman was determined, however, and offered a high price: this was accepted, and the ship returned to Falmouth the following year and had her original name restored.
sentences.translation: 然而，道曼意志坚定，报出了高价；报价获接受，船于次年返回法尔茅斯并恢复原名。
sentences.structure: however 标明执着与前次失败的反差；冒号后说明高价获接受及船返航复名的连锁结果。

sentences.text: Dowman used Cutty Sark as a training ship, and she continued in this role after his death.
sentences.translation: 道曼把卡蒂萨克号用作训练船，他去世后它仍继续承担这一角色。
sentences.structure: 主干 Dowman used... 与 she continued... 并列；after his death 突出训练用途跨越船主去世。

sentences.text: When she was no longer required, in 1954, she was transferred to dry dock at Greenwich to go on public display.
sentences.translation: 1954年它不再被需要，于是被转移到格林尼治的干船坞公开展出。
sentences.structure: When 从句交代不再需要；被动主干 was transferred，介词短语 to dry dock 说明转移目的地，只有 to go on public display 是不定式目的状语。

sentences.text: The ship suffered from fire in 2007, and again, less seriously, in 2014, but now Cutty Sark attracts a quarter of a million visitors a year.
sentences.translation: 这艘船在2007年遭遇火灾，2014年又遭遇一次较轻的火灾；如今卡蒂萨克号每年吸引25万游客。
sentences.structure: but 连接两次火灾与如今盛况的逆转；less seriously 插入比较严重程度，a quarter of a million 量化年客流。

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 2
readingSections.subtitle: More than a third of the Earth’s top layer is at risk. Is there hope for our planet’s most precious resource?
paragraphs: More than a third of the world’s soil is endangered, according to a recent UN report. If we don’t slow the decline, all farmable soil could be gone in 60 years. Since soil grows 95% of our food, and sustains human life in other more surprising ways, that is a huge problem.

Peter Groffman, from the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York, points out that soil scientists have been warning about the degradation of the world’s soil for decades. At the same time, our understanding of its importance to humans has grown. A single gram of healthy soil might contain 100 million bacteria, as well as other microorganisms such as viruses and fungi, living amid decomposing plants and various minerals. That means soils do not just grow our food, but are the source of nearly all our existing antibiotics, and could be our best hope in the fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Soil is also an ally against climate change: as microorganisms within soil digest dead animals and plants, they lock in their carbon content, holding three times the amount of carbon as does the entire atmosphere. Soils also store water, preventing flood damage: in the UK, damage to buildings, roads and bridges from floods caused by soil degradation costs £233 million every year.

If the soil loses its ability to perform these functions, the human race could be in big trouble. The danger is not that the soil will disappear completely, but that the microorganisms that give it its special properties will be lost. And once this has happened, it may take the soil thousands of years to recover. Agriculture is by far the biggest problem. In the wild, when plants grow they remove nutrients from the soil, but then when the plants die and decay these nutrients are returned directly to the soil. Humans tend not to return unused parts of harvested crops directly to the soil to enrich it, meaning that the soil gradually becomes less fertile. In the past we developed strategies to get around the problem, such as regularly varying the types of crops grown, or leaving fields uncultivated for a season.

But these practices became inconvenient as populations grew and agriculture had to be run on more commercial lines. A solution came in the early 20th century with the Haber-Bosch process for manufacturing ammonium nitrate. Farmers have been putting this synthetic fertiliser on their fields ever since. But over the past few decades, it has become clear this wasn’t such a bright idea. Chemical fertilisers can release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere and excess is often washed away with the rain, releasing nitrogen into rivers. More recently, we have found that indiscriminate use of fertilisers hurts the soil itself, turning it acidic and salty, and degrading the soil they are supposed to nourish.

One of the people looking for a solution to this problem is Pius Floris, who started out running a tree-care business in the Netherlands, and now advises some of the world’s top soil scientists. He came to realise that the best way to ensure his trees flourished was to take care of the soil, and has developed a cocktail of beneficial bacteria, fungi and humus* to do this. Researchers at the University of Valladolid in Spain recently used this cocktail on soils destroyed by years of fertiliser overuse. When they applied Floris’s mix to the desert-like test plots, a good crop of plants emerged that were not just healthy at the surface, but had roots strong enough to pierce dirt as hard as rock. The few plants that grew in the control plots, fed with traditional fertilisers, were small and weak.

However, measures like this are not enough to solve the global soil degradation problem. To assess our options on a global scale we first need an accurate picture of what types of soil are out there, and the problems they face. That’s not easy. For one thing, there is no agreed international system for classifying soil. In an attempt to unify the different approaches, the UN has created the Global Soil Map project. Researchers from nine countries are working together to create a map linked to a database that can be fed measurements from field surveys, drone surveys, satellite imagery, lab analyses and so on to provide real-time data on the state of the soil. Within the next four years, they aim to have mapped soils worldwide to a depth of 100 metres, with the results freely accessible to all.

But this is only a first step. We need ways of presenting the problem that bring it home to governments and the wider public, says Pamela Chasek at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, in Winnipeg, Canada. ‘Most scientists don’t speak language that policy-makers can understand, and vice versa.’ Chasek and her colleagues have proposed a goal of ‘zero net land degradation’. Like the idea of carbon neutrality, it is an easily understood target that can help shape expectations and encourage action. For soils on the brink, that may be too late. Several researchers are agitating for the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils. One difficulty here is defining what these areas should conserve: areas where the greatest soil diversity is present? Or areas of unspoilt soils that could act as a future benchmark of quality? Whatever we do, if we want our soils to survive, we need to take action now.

sentences.text: More than a third of the world’s soil is endangered, according to a recent UN report.
sentences.translationZh: 联合国最近的一份报告指出，世界上超过三分之一的土壤正处于危险之中。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: A段以联合国报告的数据提出危机，according to 引出信息来源。主干是 soil is endangered。

sentences.text: If we don’t slow the decline, all farmable soil could be gone in 60 years.
sentences.translationZh: 如果我们不减缓这种退化，所有可耕种土壤都可能在六十年内消失。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 条件句 If we don’t… 给出不行动的后果；主句 all farmable soil could be gone 用 could 表示高度风险而非既成事实。

sentences.text: Since soil grows 95% of our food, and sustains human life in other more surprising ways, that is a huge problem.
sentences.translationZh: 土壤供养了我们95%的食物，并且还以其他更令人意外的方式维系着人类生命，因此这是一个极其严重的问题。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: Since 引导原因从句，and 并列 grows 与 sustains；that 回指前述六十年内可耕地消失的风险，完成段落结论。

sentences.text: Peter Groffman, from the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York, points out that soil scientists have been warning about the degradation of the world’s soil for decades.
sentences.translationZh: 纽约卡里生态系统研究所的彼得·格罗夫曼指出，几十年来，土壤科学家一直在警告世人全球土壤正在退化。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 Peter Groffman points out that…；两个逗号之间是来源说明，宾语从句用现在完成进行时突出警告持续了几十年。

sentences.text: At the same time, our understanding of its importance to humans has grown.
sentences.translationZh: 与此同时，我们对土壤之于人类的重要性的认识也在加深。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: At the same time 承接“长期警告”，主干 understanding has grown，说明认知也在同步变化。

sentences.text: A single gram of healthy soil might contain 100 million bacteria, as well as other microorganisms such as viruses and fungi, living amid decomposing plants and various minerals.
sentences.translationZh: 仅一克健康土壤就可能含有一亿个细菌，还有病毒和真菌等其他微生物，它们生活在正在分解的植物和各种矿物质之间。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 A single gram… might contain…；as well as 添加微生物，living amid… 是现在分词短语，描写它们的生存环境。

sentences.text: That means soils do not just grow our food, but are the source of nearly all our existing antibiotics, and could be our best hope in the fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
sentences.translationZh: 这意味着，土壤不仅为我们生产食物，还是几乎所有现有抗生素的来源，并且可能是我们对抗耐抗生素细菌的最大希望。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: That means 引出推论；not just…but…建立递进，and could be…继续补充土壤的潜在医学价值。

sentences.text: Soil is also an ally against climate change: as microorganisms within soil digest dead animals and plants, they lock in their carbon content, holding three times the amount of carbon as does the entire atmosphere.
sentences.translationZh: 土壤也是应对气候变化的盟友：土壤中的微生物消化死亡的动植物时，会锁住其中的碳，使土壤所含的碳达到整个大气层含碳量的三倍。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 冒号后解释 ally 的具体机制；as 引导时间从句，holding… 是结果性分词结构，倒装 as does the entire atmosphere 用于比较。

sentences.text: Soils also store water, preventing flood damage: in the UK, damage to buildings, roads and bridges from floods caused by soil degradation costs £233 million every year.
sentences.translationZh: 土壤还会储存水分，从而防止洪灾损失：在英国，土壤退化引发的洪水每年给建筑物、道路和桥梁造成2.33亿英镑的损失。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 Soils store water；preventing…说明结果，冒号后的英国数据把抽象功能转化为可量化损失。

sentences.text: If the soil loses its ability to perform these functions, the human race could be in big trouble.
sentences.translationZh: 如果土壤失去履行这些功能的能力，人类就可能陷入大麻烦。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: If 引导条件；主句用 could be in big trouble 概括失去生态功能的严重后果。

sentences.text: The danger is not that the soil will disappear completely, but that the microorganisms that give it its special properties will be lost.
sentences.translationZh: 危险并不在于土壤会彻底消失，而在于赋予土壤特殊性质的微生物将会消失。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: not…but…纠正常见误解；两个 that 从句分别说明被否定的危险和真正危险。

sentences.text: And once this has happened, it may take the soil thousands of years to recover.
sentences.translationZh: 而一旦发生这种情况，土壤可能需要数千年才能恢复。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: once 引导时间兼条件关系；may take…to recover 强调恢复所需时间极其漫长。

sentences.text: Agriculture is by far the biggest problem.
sentences.translationZh: 农业是迄今为止最大的问题。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 短句单独成段内转折，用 by far 强烈排序，把危机归因转向农业。

sentences.text: In the wild, when plants grow they remove nutrients from the soil, but then when the plants die and decay these nutrients are returned directly to the soil.
sentences.translationZh: 在野外，植物生长时会从土壤中吸收养分；但植物死亡、腐烂后，这些养分又会直接回到土壤中。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: when…but then when…构成自然循环；remove 与 are returned 对照养分离开和回归土壤。

sentences.text: Humans tend not to return unused parts of harvested crops directly to the soil to enrich it, meaning that the soil gradually becomes less fertile.
sentences.translationZh: 人类往往不会把收获后未利用的作物部分直接还给土壤来使其肥沃，这意味着土壤会逐渐变得不那么肥沃。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 Humans tend not to return…；to enrich it 表目的，meaning…说明长期结果。

sentences.text: In the past we developed strategies to get around the problem, such as regularly varying the types of crops grown, or leaving fields uncultivated for a season.
sentences.translationZh: 过去，我们制定过一些绕开这个问题的策略，例如定期轮换作物种类，或让田地休耕一季。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 we developed strategies；to get around…说明策略目的，such as 后列举轮作与休耕。

sentences.text: But these practices became inconvenient as populations grew and agriculture had to be run on more commercial lines.
sentences.translationZh: 但是，随着人口增长、农业不得不更多地按商业模式经营，这些做法变得不便。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: But 承上转折；as 引导原因/伴随背景，had to be run 是被动语态，on more commercial lines 说明经营方式。

sentences.text: A solution came in the early 20th century with the Haber-Bosch process for manufacturing ammonium nitrate.
sentences.translationZh: 二十世纪初，制造硝酸铵的哈伯—博施法带来了一种解决办法。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 A solution came；with…引出具体技术，for manufacturing…说明工艺用途。

sentences.text: Farmers have been putting this synthetic fertiliser on their fields ever since.
sentences.translationZh: 从那以后，农民一直把这种合成肥料施到田地里。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 现在完成进行时 have been putting 强调从发明以来持续到现在的施肥行为。

sentences.text: But over the past few decades, it has become clear this wasn’t such a bright idea.
sentences.translationZh: 然而在过去几十年里，人们已经清楚地认识到，这并不是一个多么明智的主意。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: But 转折否定上一段的“解决办法”；形式主语 it 后的 that 被省略，bright idea 带克制的反讽。

vocabulary.meaning: 明智的主意（此处带反讽）

sentences.text: Chemical fertilisers can release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere and excess is often washed away with the rain, releasing nitrogen into rivers.
sentences.translationZh: 化肥会向大气释放具有污染性的氧化亚氮，而过量的肥料常被雨水冲走，将氮释放进河流。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: and 连接两种污染路径；releasing…说明肥料被冲走后的结果。

sentences.text: More recently, we have found that indiscriminate use of fertilisers hurts the soil itself, turning it acidic and salty, and degrading the soil they are supposed to nourish.
sentences.translationZh: 最近我们还发现，不加选择地使用肥料会伤害土壤本身，使其变酸、变咸，并让本应得到滋养的土壤退化。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: that 引导宾语从句；turning、degrading 两个并列分词说明伤害形式，they are supposed to nourish 是关系从句并形成反讽。

sentences.text: One of the people looking for a solution to this problem is Pius Floris, who started out running a tree-care business in the Netherlands, and now advises some of the world’s top soil scientists.
sentences.translationZh: 寻找这一问题解决办法的人中有一位叫皮乌斯·弗洛里斯；他起初在荷兰经营树木养护业务，如今则为一些世界顶尖的土壤科学家提供建议。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 One…is Pius Floris；who 引导非限制性定语从句，started out…与 now advises…形成职业转变。

sentences.text: He came to realise that the best way to ensure his trees flourished was to take care of the soil, and has developed a cocktail of beneficial bacteria, fungi and humus* to do this.
sentences.translationZh: 他开始意识到，要保证树木茁壮生长，最好的办法就是照料土壤；为此，他研制出一种由有益细菌、真菌和腐殖质组成的混合制剂。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 He came to realise…and has developed…；that 从句说明认识，to ensure…表目的，was to take care…作表语。

vocabulary.meaning: 由多种成分组成的混合物

sentences.text: Researchers at the University of Valladolid in Spain recently used this cocktail on soils destroyed by years of fertiliser overuse.
sentences.translationZh: 西班牙巴利亚多利德大学的研究人员最近把这种混合制剂用于因多年过度施肥而遭到破坏的土壤。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 Researchers…used this cocktail；destroyed by…是过去分词短语，说明土壤受损原因。

vocabulary.meaning: 混合制剂；多种成分的混合物（本篇再次出现）

sentences.text: When they applied Floris’s mix to the desert-like test plots, a good crop of plants emerged that were not just healthy at the surface, but had roots strong enough to pierce dirt as hard as rock.
sentences.translationZh: 他们把弗洛里斯的混合物施到沙漠般的试验地后，长出了一片长势良好的作物：它们不仅地表部分健康，根系也足够强壮，能够刺穿坚如岩石的泥土。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: When 引导时间从句；主句 a good crop…emerged，that 从句用 not just…but…对照地表健康与根系强度。

sentences.text: The few plants that grew in the control plots, fed with traditional fertilisers, were small and weak.
sentences.translationZh: 对照试验地中用传统肥料培育出来的少数植物又小又弱。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干是 The few plants…were small and weak；that grew…修饰 plants；fed with traditional fertilisers 是过去分词短语，表示植物接受传统肥料处理，而非植物主动施肥。

sentences.text: However, measures like this are not enough to solve the global soil degradation problem.
sentences.translationZh: 然而，类似措施不足以解决全球性的土壤退化问题。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: However 把局部试验拉回全球尺度；not enough to solve 表明该办法有成效但不足以成为完整答案。

sentences.text: To assess our options on a global scale we first need an accurate picture of what types of soil are out there, and the problems they face.
sentences.translationZh: 要在全球范围内评估我们的选择，首先需要准确了解有哪些土壤类型，以及它们各自面临什么问题。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 句首不定式 To assess…表目的；主干 we need an accurate picture，两个 of/what 结构说明需要掌握的内容。

sentences.text: That’s not easy.
sentences.translationZh: 这并不容易。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 极短句承接上一句，制造停顿，准备列出全球评估困难。

sentences.text: For one thing, there is no agreed international system for classifying soil.
sentences.translationZh: 首先，国际上并没有一套公认的土壤分类体系。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: For one thing 表示先列一个理由；there is no…指出制度层面的分类障碍。

sentences.text: In an attempt to unify the different approaches, the UN has created the Global Soil Map project.
sentences.translationZh: 为了统一不同方法，联合国创建了“全球土壤地图”项目。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: In an attempt to…表目的；主干 the UN has created…说明全球项目对此作出的回应。

sentences.text: Researchers from nine countries are working together to create a map linked to a database that can be fed measurements from field surveys, drone surveys, satellite imagery, lab analyses and so on to provide real-time data on the state of the soil.
sentences.translationZh: 来自九个国家的研究人员正在合作绘制一幅与数据库相连的地图；数据库可接收实地调查、无人机调查、卫星图像、实验室分析等测量资料，从而提供土壤状况的实时数据。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 Researchers…are working…；linked to…修饰 map，that can be fed…修饰 database，to provide…表目的。

sentences.text: Within the next four years, they aim to have mapped soils worldwide to a depth of 100 metres, with the results freely accessible to all.
sentences.translationZh: 他们的目标是在未来四年内绘制出全球深至100米的土壤地图，并让所有人都能免费获取结果。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 they aim；to have mapped 是完成式不定式，强调四年期限内完成；with…补充结果的开放性。

sentences.text: But this is only a first step.
sentences.translationZh: 但这仅仅是第一步。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: But 表明绘图仍非终点；only 限缩其意义并引出传播和政策行动。

sentences.text: We need ways of presenting the problem that bring it home to governments and the wider public, says Pamela Chasek at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, in Winnipeg, Canada.
sentences.translationZh: 加拿大温尼伯国际可持续发展研究所的帕梅拉·蔡塞克说，我们需要用一些方式呈现问题，让政府和更广泛的公众切身理解它。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 We need ways；of presenting…修饰 ways，that bring…修饰 problem；句末 says…是引语来源倒装。

sentences.text: ‘Most scientists don’t speak language that policy-makers can understand, and vice versa.’
sentences.translationZh: “大多数科学家不会说政策制定者能听懂的语言，反过来也一样。”
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 直接引语用 and vice versa 概括科学界与政策界之间的双向沟通鸿沟。

sentences.text: Chasek and her colleagues have proposed a goal of ‘zero net land degradation’.
sentences.translationZh: 蔡塞克和她的同事提出了“土地净退化为零”的目标。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 Chasek and her colleagues have proposed…；引号标示一个便于传播的政策目标。

sentences.text: Like the idea of carbon neutrality, it is an easily understood target that can help shape expectations and encourage action.
sentences.translationZh: 就像“碳中和”的理念一样，这是一个容易理解的目标，可以帮助塑造预期并促进行动。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: Like…作比较状语；主干 it is a target，that 从句说明目标如何影响预期并促进行动。

sentences.text: For soils on the brink, that may be too late.
sentences.translationZh: 对于濒临崩溃的土壤来说，那也许已经太晚了。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 介词短语 For soils on the brink 限定对象；that 回指前述容易理解的目标和由此推动的行动。

sentences.text: Several researchers are agitating for the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils.
sentences.translationZh: 几位研究人员正在积极呼吁立即为濒危土壤建立保护区。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 现在进行时 are agitating 强调呼吁正在发生；for 后接要立即建立保护区的诉求。

sentences.text: One difficulty here is defining what these areas should conserve: areas where the greatest soil diversity is present?
sentences.translationZh: 这里的一个难题是要界定这些区域应该保护什么：是土壤多样性最丰富的地区吗？
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 主干 One difficulty is defining…；冒号把抽象的“保护什么”展开为第一个选择。

sentences.text: Or areas of unspoilt soils that could act as a future benchmark of quality?
sentences.translationZh: 还是可以作为未来质量基准的未受破坏土壤区域？
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: 省略式疑问句与上一句并列，提出以未受破坏土壤作为未来质量参照的第二种标准。

sentences.text: Whatever we do, if we want our soils to survive, we need to take action now.
sentences.translationZh: 无论采取什么办法，如果想让土壤存续下去，我们现在就必须行动。
sentences.syntaxAndFunctionZh: Whatever 引导让步从句，if 引导条件；主句 need to take action now 以紧迫行动收束全文。

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 3
readingSections.titleText: Book Review: The Happiness Industry: How the Government and Big Business Sold Us Well-Being
readingSections.subtitle: Book Review
paragraphs: ‘Happiness is the ultimate goal because it is self-evidently good. If we are asked why happiness matters we can give no further external reason. It just obviously does matter.’ This pronouncement by Richard Layard, an economist and advocate of ‘positive psychology’, summarises the beliefs of many people today. For Layard and others like him, it is obvious that the purpose of government is to promote a state of collective well-being. The only question is how to achieve it, and here positive psychology – a supposed science that not only identifies what makes people happy but also allows their happiness to be measured – can show the way. Equipped with this science, they say, governments can secure happiness in society in a way they never could in the past.

It is an astonishingly crude and simple-minded way of thinking, and for that very reason increasingly popular. Those who think in this way are oblivious to the vast philosophical literature in which the meaning and value of happiness have been explored and questioned, and write as if nothing of any importance had been thought on the subject until it came to their attention. It was the philosopher Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) who was more than anyone else responsible for the development of this way of thinking. For Bentham it was obvious that the human good consists of pleasure and the absence of pain. The Greek philosopher Aristotle may have identified happiness with self-realisation in the 4th century BC, and thinkers throughout the ages may have struggled to reconcile the pursuit of happiness with other human values, but for Bentham all this was mere metaphysics or fiction. Without knowing anything much of him or the school of moral theory he established – since they are by education and intellectual conviction illiterate in the history of ideas – our advocates of positive psychology follow in his tracks in rejecting as outmoded and irrelevant pretty much the entirety of ethical reflection on human happiness to date.

But as William Davies notes in his recent book The Happiness Industry, the view that happiness is the only self-evident good is actually a way of limiting moral inquiry. One of the virtues of this rich, lucid and arresting book is that it places the current cult of happiness in a well-defined historical framework. Rightly, Davies begins his story with Bentham, noting that he was far more than a philosopher. Davies writes, ‘Bentham’s activities were those which we might now associate with a public sector management consultant’. In the 1790s, he wrote to the Home Office suggesting that the departments of government be linked together through a set of ‘conversation tubes’, and to the Bank of England with a design for a printing device that could produce unforgeable banknotes. He drew up plans for a ‘frigidarium’ to keep provisions such as meat, fish, fruit and vegetables fresh. His celebrated design for a prison to be known as a ‘Panopticon’, in which prisoners would be kept in solitary confinement while being visible at all times to the guards, was very nearly adopted. (Surprisingly, Davies does not discuss the fact that Bentham meant his Panopticon not just as a model prison but also as an instrument of control that could be applied to schools and factories.)

Bentham was also a pioneer of the ‘science of happiness’. If happiness is to be regarded as a science, it has to be measured, and Bentham suggested two ways in which this might be done. Viewing happiness as a complex of pleasurable sensations, he suggested that it might be quantified by measuring the human pulse rate. Alternatively, money could be used as the standard for quantification: if two different goods have the same price, it can be claimed that they produce the same quantity of pleasure in the consumer. Bentham was more attracted by the latter measure. By associating money so closely to inner experience, Davies writes, Bentham ‘set the stage for the entangling of psychological research and capitalism that would shape the business practices of the twentieth century’.

The Happiness Industry describes how the project of a science of happiness has become integral to capitalism. We learn much that is interesting about how economic problems are being redefined and treated as psychological maladies. In addition, Davies shows how the belief that inner states of pleasure and displeasure can be objectively measured has informed management studies and advertising. The tendency of thinkers such as J B Watson, the founder of behaviourism*, was that human beings could be shaped, or manipulated, by policymakers and managers. Watson had no factual basis for his view of human action. When he became president of the American Psychological Association in 1915, he ‘had never even studied a single human being’: his research had been confined to experiments on white rats. Yet Watson’s reductive model is now widely applied, with ‘behaviour change’ becoming the goal of governments: in Britain, a ‘Behaviour Insights Team’ has been established by the government to study how people can be encouraged, at minimum cost to the public purse, to live in what are considered to be socially desirable ways.

Modern industrial societies appear to need the possibility of ever-increasing happiness to motivate them in their labours. But whatever its intellectual pedigree, the idea that governments should be responsible for promoting happiness is always a threat to human freedom.

questions.evidence: A solution came in the early 20th century with the Haber-Bosch process for manufacturing ammonium nitrate. Farmers have been putting this synthetic fertiliser on their fields ever since. Chemical fertilisers can release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere and excess is often washed away with the rain, releasing nitrogen into rivers. More recently, we have found that indiscriminate use of fertilisers hurts the soil itself, turning it acidic and salty, and degrading the soil they are supposed to nourish.
questions.logicZh: 句18引入 Haber-Bosch 工艺制造硝酸铵，句19把其产物明确称为 synthetic fertiliser；句21–22再说明这类 chemical fertilisers 会污染大气、河流并伤害土壤，因此对应 E“损害环境的不同方面”。
questions.distractorsZh: A 是弗洛里斯混合物的效果；C 是作物残余养分；D 是政策目标；F 没有原文依据；B 与土壤数据库有关。

questions.evidence: We need ways of presenting the problem that bring it home to governments and the wider public, says Pamela Chasek at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, in Winnipeg, Canada. Chasek and her colleagues have proposed a goal of ‘zero net land degradation’. Like the idea of carbon neutrality, it is an easily understood target that can help shape expectations and encourage action.
questions.logicZh: 句36先提出要让 governments and the wider public 切身理解土壤问题；句38–39随即提出易懂的“零净土地退化”目标，用来塑造预期并促进行动，完整支持 D“帮助政府更充分意识到土壤问题”。

questions.stem: examples of different ways of collecting information on soil degradation

questions.evidence: Researchers from nine countries are working together to create a map linked to a database that can be fed measurements from field surveys, drone surveys, satellite imagery, lab analyses and so on to provide real-time data on the state of the soil.
questions.logicZh: field surveys、drone surveys、satellite imagery、lab analyses 是四种采集资料的方法。
questions.distractorsZh: A：只说明土壤危机规模与食物风险，没有信息采集方式；B：列举土壤成分和生态功能，没有说明如何采集退化数据；C：解释自然养分循环和农业造成的退化，没有调查方法清单；D：讨论合成肥料及污染，没有数据采集方法；E：描述弗洛里斯的单项修复试验，不是多种信息收集方式；G：讨论公共沟通、政策目标和保护区，没有调查技术。F 才并列 field surveys、drone surveys、satellite imagery、lab analyses。

questions.stem: a suggestion for a way of keeping some types of soil safe in the near future
questions.translationZh: 提出一种在近期保护某些土壤类型的方法
questions.evidence: Several researchers are agitating for the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils.
questions.logicZh: immediate 对应 in the near future；protected zones for endangered soils 即保护某些土壤的办法。
questions.distractorsZh: A：只报告土壤面临危险，没有提出保护办法；B：说明健康土壤的价值和功能，没有近期保护建议；C：解释农业如何消耗养分，没有保护特定土壤的制度措施；D：讨论化肥产生与危害，没有建立保护区；E：用微生物混合物修复试验地，不是让某些土壤在近期免受破坏的保护区方案；F：全球测绘用于掌握土壤状况，不直接保护特定土壤。G 的 immediate creation of protected zones 才符合题意。

questions.evidence: For one thing, there is no agreed international system for classifying soil.
questions.logicZh: 要形成 accurate picture/overview，必须统一分类；没有公认国际分类体系正是困难原因。
questions.distractorsZh: A：给出危机比例和六十年风险，没有解释为何难以形成全球概览；B：说明土壤成分和功能，没有讨论分类或概览障碍；C：说明农业退化机制，没有全球信息整合困难；D：说明化肥危害，没有概览方法问题；E：说明局部修复试验，没有解释全球概览困难；G：困难在于让政府公众切身理解问题以及界定保护对象，不是形成土壤退化全貌。F 明确指出没有公认的国际土壤分类体系。

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer’s attitude to advocates of positive psychology?
questions.translationZh: 评论者对积极心理学倡导者持什么态度？

options.label: A
options.text: They are wrong to reject the ideas of Bentham.
options.translationZh: 他们拒绝边沁的思想是错误的。

options.label: B
options.text: They are over-influenced by their study of Bentham’s theories.
options.translationZh: 他们因研究边沁理论而受其过度影响。

options.label: C
options.text: They have a fresh new approach to ideas on human happiness.
options.translationZh: 他们以全新方式看待人类幸福。

options.label: D
options.text: They are ignorant about the ideas they should be considering.
options.translationZh: 他们不了解本应纳入考虑的思想。

questions.evidence: our advocates of positive psychology ... are ... illiterate in the history of ideas
questions.reasoning: illiterate in the history of ideas直接对应ignorant about the ideas。
questions.distractors: A错误：作者不是批评他们拒绝边沁，而是说他们不自知地追随边沁；B错误：他们对边沁所知甚少，并非受深入研究过度影响；C错误：作者说他们忽视思想史，并非赞扬其新颖；D正确：illiterate in the history of ideas 对应 ignorant about the ideas。

questions.prompt: The reviewer refers to the Greek philosopher Aristotle in order to suggest that happiness
questions.translationZh: 评论者提到希腊哲学家亚里士多德，是为了说明幸福……

options.label: A
options.text: may not be just pleasure and the absence of pain.
options.translationZh: 可能不只是快乐和没有痛苦。

options.label: B
options.text: should not be the main goal of humans.
options.translationZh: 不应成为人类的主要目标。

options.label: C
options.text: is not something that should be fought for.
options.translationZh: 不是应当争取的东西。

options.label: D
options.text: is not just an abstract concept.
options.translationZh: 不只是抽象概念。

questions.evidence: Aristotle may have identified happiness with self-realisation ... but for Bentham all this was mere metaphysics
questions.reasoning: 亚里士多德以自我实现界定幸福，显示幸福不只等于快乐且无痛苦。
questions.distractors: A正确：self-realisation证明幸福不只等于快乐且无痛；B错误：原文没有说幸福不应成为主要目标；C错误：原文没有反对争取幸福；D错误：此处比较幸福定义，而非抽象与具体。

questions.prompt: According to Davies, Bentham’s suggestion for linking the price of goods to happiness was significant because
questions.translationZh: 据戴维斯说，边沁把商品价格与幸福联系起来的建议之所以重要，是因为……

options.label: A
options.text: it was the first successful way of assessing happiness.
options.translationZh: 这是首个成功评估幸福的方法。

options.label: B
options.text: it established a connection between work and psychology.
options.translationZh: 它在商业活动与心理学之间建立了联系。

options.label: C
options.text: it was the first successful example of psychological research.
options.translationZh: 这是心理学研究首次成功的例子。

options.label: D
options.text: it involved consideration of the rights of consumers.
options.translationZh: 它涉及对消费者权利的考虑。

questions.evidence: set the stage for the entangling of psychological research and capitalism that would shape the business practices
questions.reasoning: psychological research与capitalism/business practices的联系对应B。
questions.distractors: A错误：原文未称这是首个成功评估方法；B正确：对应心理研究与资本主义商业实践的联结；C错误：原文未称其为首个成功心理研究；D错误：全文没有讨论消费者权利。

questions.prompt: technology to improve __________ for different Government departments
questions.translationZh: 改善不同政府部门之间的__________的技术
questions.evidence: departments of government be linked together through a set of ‘conversation tubes’
questions.distractors: A measurement属于幸福量化；B security属于纸币防伪；C implementation无原文对应；D profits无原文对应；E observation属于监狱监视；F communication正确；G preservation属于食物保鲜。

questions.prompt: a new way of printing banknotes to increase __________
questions.translationZh: 新的纸币印刷方式，以提高__________
questions.evidence: a printing device that could produce unforgeable banknotes
questions.distractors: A measurement不等于防伪；B security正确；C implementation未提；D profits未提；E observation对应监狱监视；F communication对应部门联络；G preservation对应食物保鲜。

questions.prompt: a method for the __________ of food
questions.translationZh: 一种用于食物__________的方法
questions.evidence: a ‘frigidarium’ to keep provisions ... fresh
questions.distractors: A measurement对应幸福量化；B security对应纸币防伪；C implementation未提；D profits未提；E observation对应监狱监视；F communication对应部门联络；G preservation正确，对应keep ... fresh。

questions.prompt: a prison which allowed the __________ of prisoners at all times
questions.translationZh: 一座允许随时__________囚犯的监狱
questions.evidence: prisoners would be ... visible at all times to the guards
questions.distractors: A measurement对应幸福量化；B security不是该监狱设计在此强调的功能；C implementation未提；D profits未提；E observation正确；F communication对应部门联络；G preservation对应食物保鲜。

questions.prompt: possibilities for its __________
questions.translationZh: 对幸福进行__________的可能性
questions.evidence: If happiness is to be regarded as a science, it has to be measured
questions.distractors: A measurement正确；B security是纸币防伪；C implementation未提；D profits不是文中的价格衡量；E observation是监狱监视；F communication是部门联络；G preservation是食物保鲜。

questions.prompt: One strength of The Happiness Industry is its discussion of the relationship between psychology and economics.
questions.translationZh: 《幸福产业》的一个优点是讨论了心理学与经济学之间的关系。
questions.evidence: One of the virtues ...; ... entangling of psychological research and capitalism; ... economic problems ... psychological maladies
questions.reasoning: 作者称书有virtues，并肯定其揭示心理研究与资本主义/经济问题的关系。
questions.distractors: NO与称赞相反；NOT GIVEN不成立，因为关系被明确讨论。

questions.prompt: It is more difficult to measure some emotions than others.
questions.translationZh: 有些情绪比另一些更难测量。
questions.evidence: Viewing happiness as a complex of pleasurable sensations, he suggested that it might be quantified by measuring the human pulse rate. / In addition, Davies shows how the belief that inner states of pleasure and displeasure can be objectively measured has informed management studies and advertising.
questions.reasoning: 两处只讨论幸福或愉悦/不悦可被测量，没有比较some emotions与others的测量难度。
questions.distractors: YES不成立：可测量性不能推出不同情绪难度有别；NO不成立：原文也没有说所有情绪同样容易；NOT GIVEN正确：缺少比较维度。

questions.prompt: Watson’s ideas on behaviourism were supported by research on humans he carried out before 1915.
questions.translationZh: 沃森关于行为主义的观点得到了他在1915年前开展的人体研究的支持。
questions.evidence: he ‘had never even studied a single human being’: his research had been confined to experiments on white rats
questions.reasoning: 题干称有人体研究；原文明确从未研究人，只研究白鼠。
questions.distractors: YES与原文相反；NOT GIVEN不成立，因为研究对象明确。

questions.prompt: Watson’s ideas have been most influential on governments outside America.
questions.translationZh: 沃森的思想对美国以外的政府影响最大。
questions.evidence: Yet Watson’s reductive model is now widely applied, with ‘behaviour change’ becoming the goal of governments: in Britain, a ‘Behaviour Insights Team’ has been established by the government to study how people can be encouraged, at minimum cost to the public purse, to live in what are considered to be socially desirable ways.
questions.reasoning: 原文只举英国实例，没有比较美国内外的影响程度，更没有most influential最高级依据。
questions.distractors: YES不成立：英国例子不能推出美国以外影响最大；NO不成立：原文也未说美国影响更大；NOT GIVEN正确：缺少地域与程度比较。

questions.prompt: The need for happiness is linked to industrialisation.
questions.translationZh: 对幸福的需要与工业化有关。
questions.evidence: Modern industrial societies appear to need the possibility of ever-increasing happiness to motivate them in their labours.
questions.reasoning: industrial societies与need ... happiness直接建立联系。
questions.distractors: NO与原句相反；NOT GIVEN不成立，因为联系明确。

questions.prompt: A main aim of government should be to increase the happiness of the population.
questions.translationZh: 政府的一项主要目标应是提高民众幸福。
questions.evidence: the idea that governments should be responsible for promoting happiness is always a threat to human freedom
questions.reasoning: 作者认为政府负责促进幸福会威胁自由，与题干应当如此相反。
questions.distractors: YES混淆Layard的主张与评论者立场；NOT GIVEN不成立，因为末句明确表态。
